description: Faithful reproduction of OpenClaw's agent-side architecture for CUA. Six components (B1-B6) across three phases: Phase 1 builds independent modules (prompt builder, memory, session persistence), Phase 2 adds context management and tool wiring, Phase 3 integrates everything into the agent loop. IMPORTANT: Category C components (CUA SDK callbacks like ImageRetentionCallback, TrajectorySaverCallback, BudgetManagerCallback, PromptInstructionsCallback) are assumed directly reusable from the CUA SDK without modification. This assumption may be wrong — these callbacks may have undocumented constraints, incompatible hook signatures, ordering dependencies, or behavioral quirks when combined with our custom callbacks. Every story that uses a Category C component must verify it works as expected during integration, not just assume it. If a CUA callback doesn't behave as needed, file an issue and implement a workaround or replacement in agents/openclaw/ rather than patching the CUA SDK.

userStories.notes: File: agents/openclaw/tools.py. Two components: 1) build_tools(session, memory_store) -> list — assembles [session._computer, MilestoneTool(session.interface), MemorySearchTool(store), MemoryGetTool(store), MemoryWriteTool(store)]. 2) ToolLoggingCallback(AsyncCallbackHandler) — implements on_function_call_start(item) to log tool name + truncated params, on_function_call_end(item, result) to log tool name + result summary + duration. Keep it simple — this is a thin assembly layer, not a policy engine. OpenClaw's tool policy system (approval chains, sandbox rules, subagent restrictions) is irrelevant for CUA where all tools are pre-approved.

Level 2: run_magic_tower.sh 50 — with ALL Category C callbacks enabled (ImageRetention, TrajectorySaver, BudgetManager, PromptInstructions, Logging), verify no conflicts or silent failures

Level 2: TrajectorySaverCallback — verify trajectory directory contains expected files (metadata.json, turn_NNN/ dirs with screenshots and response JSONs)

Level 2: ComputerAgent vs Pi agent core — CRITICAL: verify ComputerAgent's run loop (message accumulation, tool dispatch, step yielding) is equivalent to Pi's embedded runner for our use case. Specifically check: (a) how messages accumulate across steps (does ComputerAgent maintain a growing message list like Pi, or does it manage its own truncation?), (b) whether on_llm_start receives the full message history or just the delta, (c) whether our callbacks can intercept and modify the message list before each LLM call (needed for compaction injection), (d) how tool results are appended to context (needed for tool result truncation). Document any gaps.
userStories.notes: CAVEAT: The A/B/C classification was done upfront from source analysis, not runtime evidence. Components may be miscategorized or overlooked — acceptance criteria are subject to change. Treat component lists as starting points, not exhaustive. Verification-only story — no new code unless issues are found. For each Category C component: read its source, run a VM test with it enabled, check trajectory/logs. Document issues in docs/category-c-audit.md. HIGHEST-RISK ITEM: ComputerAgent as Pi agent core equivalent. Explore ComputerAgent.run() and the active agent loop end-to-end — compare against openclaw/src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/ to understand gaps in message accumulation, callback interception, and tool result handling. If ComputerAgent is too inflexible, options include: custom_loop override, forking ComputerAgent, or reworking our context management approach.
